hedonism

HEE-duh-niz-um -- from Greek hedone ('pleasure') + -ism. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Hedonism is the pursuit of pleasure as life's highest or most important goal.

The documentary followed a group of retired tycoons who had built their entire post-work lives around unapologetic hedonism -- yachts, casinos, and nightly parties.

Worked Example

The philosophy professor explained that ancient hedonism wasn't just about wild parties -- some early thinkers argued that avoiding pain was just as central to the pursuit of pleasure as seeking enjoyment.

That whole worldview built around maximizing pleasure and minimizing discomfort, whether through parties or careful moderation, is exactly what hedonism describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

epicureanism: Epicureanism is devotion to refined, carefully chosen pleasure — the perfect meal, the exact right wine — prizing quality over quantity. Hedonism is broader and less picky: any pleasure counts, and what defines it is simply that pleasure sits at the center of life.

pleasure-seeking: Pleasure-seeking is the everyday habit of chasing enjoyment — booking the trip, ordering the dessert, staying for one more song. Hedonism runs deeper than a habit: it is a whole outlook, a settled belief that pleasure is what life is for.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

asceticism: a lifestyle of strict self-denial, often for spiritual reasons

austerity: extreme plainness and avoidance of luxury

Where it sits · how central pleasure is to life — indulgence → hedonism → debauchery

indulgence vs. hedonism: Indulgence is milder than hedonism: a single slice of cake after dinner is a small indulgence, while hedonism goes much further, making pleasure itself life's supreme and constant goal.

debauchery vs. hedonism: Debauchery is stronger and more destructive than hedonism: a hedonist makes pleasure life's guiding goal, while debauchery is that pursuit run to wild, ruinous excess — health, money, and judgment all thrown away for the next thrill.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hedon-

root — hedon-: pleasure (Greek (hedone))

suffix — -ism

suffix — -ism: a belief or practice; forms a noun (Greek (-ismos))

Put it together

Put it together: Greek hedone meant 'pleasure,' and the suffix -ism names a belief or practice. Hedonism is literally the practice of treating pleasure as life's guiding goal.

Use the root in a new word: anhedonia

Use the root in a new word: anhedonia: One of the most difficult symptoms of depression is anhedonia, the inability to feel pleasure in things once enjoyed.
